title: Risk management and IT security
blurb: Threats, secure systems, controls and the risks of new technology.

topics.name: Information security risks
topics.line: Mistakes, faults, nature and deliberate harm. The big clue is intent.
topics.remember: H-T-D: Human error, Technical error, Deliberate actions (fraud, espionage, malicious damage)
topics.simple: Information can be harmed by mistakes, by faults, by nature or by people who mean to do harm. The big clue is intent.
frames: Human error: an accountant enters NPR 58,000 instead of NPR 85,000.
Technical error: a server stops because of a hardware failure.
Natural disasters can also damage data.
Deliberate actions: fraud, espionage or malicious damage, done on purpose.
gls: an unintentional mistake by a person
stealing confidential business information for advantage

cards.mean: Unintentional mistakes: incorrect transactions, uncorrected errors, wrong files
cards.ex: An accountant enters NPR 58,000 instead of NPR 85,000.

cards.mean: Hardware malfunction or software failure
cards.ex: A server stops because of a hardware failure.

cards.mean: Listed with data risks on the chapter map
cards.ex: A flood damages the server room.

cards.mean: Intentional misuse of the system for gain
cards.ex: Changing supplier bank details to divert payments.

cards.mean: Stealing confidential business information for advantage
cards.ex: A competitor copies a pricing list.

cards.mean: Intentionally damaging or destroying data or systems
cards.ex: An employee deletes the accounting database.

items.q: An accountant accidentally enters 75,000 instead of 57,000
items.why: An accidental mistake by a person is human error.

items.q: The server fails because of a hardware fault
items.why: A hardware failure is a technical error.

items.q: An employee intentionally shares confidential data with a competitor
items.why: Intent makes it a deliberate action.

items.q: A flood damages the server room
items.why: Damage caused by nature is a natural disaster.

items.q: Software crashes during processing
items.why: A software failure is a technical error.

items.q: An employee changes records to commit fraud
items.why: Fraud is a deliberate action.

topics.name: Six aspects of security
topics.line: Six ways an organisation responds to threats.
topics.remember: P-D-D-R-C-T: Prevention, Detection, Deterrence, Recovery, Correction, Threat avoidance
topics.simple: When something threatens information, there are six kinds of response. Learn them in order.
frames: Prevention stops it: a password before the accounting software opens.
Detection spots it: failed logins are recorded.
Deterrence discourages it: staff are warned about discipline.
Recovery restores data from backups. Correction then fixes the weakness.
gls: fixing the weakness that allowed the threat
redesigning the system to remove the risk

cards.mean: Measures to stop threats before they happen
cards.ex: A password before the accounting software opens.

cards.mean: Identifying when a breach or attempt occurs
cards.ex: The system records failed login attempts.

cards.mean: Discouraging people from attempting breaches
cards.ex: Staff are told misuse leads to disciplinary action.

cards.mean: Restoring systems and limiting damage after a threat
cards.ex: Restoring lost records from backups.

cards.mean: Fixing the weaknesses that allowed the threat
cards.ex: Removing access when employees leave.

cards.mean: Changing the design to eliminate the risk
cards.ex: Users can no longer touch database files directly.

items.q: A password before accessing the accounting software
items.why: Stopping the incident before it happens is prevention.

items.q: The system records failed login attempts
items.why: Identifying an attempt is detection.

items.q: Warning employees of disciplinary action
items.why: Discouraging misuse is deterrence.

items.q: Restoring records from backup after a crash
items.why: Restoring what was lost is recovery.

items.q: Removing access for leavers after an audit found the gap
items.why: Fixing the weakness is correction.

items.q: Redesigning the system so users cannot touch database files
items.why: Changing the design to remove the risk is threat avoidance.

topics.name: Qualities of a secure system
topics.remember: ACIANA: Availability, Confidentiality, Integrity, Authenticity, Non-repudiation, Authorisation
topics.simple: A secure system has six qualities. Each one answers a different question about the information.
frames: Availability: can authorised people use it when needed?
Confidentiality: can only the right people see it?
Integrity: is it still accurate and unchanged?
Authorisation: can people do only what they are allowed to do?
gls: the information or user is genuine
a person cannot deny an action they performed
permission to perform a specific action

cards.mean: Accessible to authorised users when needed
cards.ex: Mobile banking works when customers need it.

cards.mean: Only authorised users can view it
cards.ex: Payroll is visible only to HR and finance.

cards.mean: Accurate and unchanged from the source
cards.ex: A deposit of NPR 50,000 stays NPR 50,000.

cards.mean: Comes from a genuine, trusted source
cards.ex: The bank checks a request really comes from the customer.

cards.mean: Users cannot deny actions they performed
cards.ex: A payment record proves who authorised it.

cards.mean: Only approved users can do specific actions
cards.ex: A junior accountant enters invoices, a manager approves payments.

items.q: Customers can use mobile banking whenever they need it
items.why: Accessible when needed is availability.

items.q: Only HR can see everyone's salary
items.why: Keeping information from unauthorised viewers is confidentiality.

items.q: Data must stay the same as its source and not be altered
items.why: Accurate and unchanged is integrity.

items.q: The bank checks a transaction truly came from the customer
items.why: Verifying a genuine source is authenticity.

items.q: A user cannot deny a payment they made
items.why: Not being able to deny an action is non-repudiation.

items.q: Only approved employees can change payroll records
items.why: Permission to act is authorisation.

nodes.s: can I use it when needed?
only the right people see it
is it from a genuine source?
a person cannot deny an action

topics.name: Physical and logical access
topics.line: Keeping unauthorised people out of rooms, systems and data.
topics.remember: Physical: P-D-I-D-P. Logical: Identification, Authentication, Authorisation (I-A-A).
topics.simple: Physical controls protect rooms and equipment. Logical controls protect systems and data.
frames: A guard checks identification at reception.
A keypad or card opens the server room door.
An alarm sounds if someone enters without permission.
On the computer, identification, authentication and authorisation guard the data.
gls: stops unauthorised people entering IT facilities
proving you are who you claim to be
a unique number that identifies a person and records entry

cards.mean: People such as guards and receptionists manage entry
cards.ex: A receptionist checks ID before letting a visitor in.

cards.mean: Mechanisms, with keypads or cards, for areas with low entry traffic
cards.ex: The server room opens only with an authorised card.

cards.mean: Alarms triggered by unauthorised access attempts
cards.ex: A sensor alerts security when someone enters at midnight.

cards.mean: Protects laptops, tablets and phones from theft or misuse
cards.ex: Laptops are stored securely after work.

cards.mean: A unique PIN identifies people and keeps access records
cards.ex: Entry to the server room is logged with the PIN and time.

cards.mean: Who is trying to access?
cards.ex: A username such as Nitesh01.

cards.mean: Prove you are who you claim to be
cards.ex: The correct password.

cards.mean: What are you permitted to do?
cards.ex: An accountant sees accounting records, HR sees employee records.

items.q: A receptionist checks a visitor's ID
items.why: A person managing entry is a personnel control.

items.q: A keypad on the server room door
items.why: A keypad is a door lock and entry system.

items.q: A motion sensor detects entry after hours
items.why: Detecting unauthorised entry is the job of an intruder alarm.

items.q: Laptops locked away when not in use
items.why: Protecting devices from theft is device security.

items.q: A unique number recorded with the entry time
items.why: A unique number that identifies people and logs entry is a PIN.

topics.name: Integrity controls
topics.line: Checking data as it goes in, is processed and comes out.
topics.remember: Verification = against the source. Validation = against the rules. Check digits are validation.
topics.simple: Integrity means data is complete and not corrupted. We check it as it goes in, while it is processed and when it comes out.
frames: Verification compares what was typed with the original document.
Validation applies programmed rules, such as a sensible range.
Totals help show if anything is missing.
Output controls check reports and who receives them.
gls: matching entered data with the source document
programmed checks that data is reasonable
a group of transactions processed together

cards.mean: Complete and not corrupted
cards.ex: An invoice recorded in full at the right amount.

cards.mean: Entered data matches the source documents
cards.ex: Compare the system entry with the original invoice.

cards.mean: Programmed checks that data is reasonable and not incomplete
cards.ex: The system rejects an age of 250.

cards.mean: A form of validation, not verification
cards.ex: The computer applies a rule. No source document is compared.

cards.mean: Ensures accuracy
cards.ex: A calculated digit added to a code to catch entry errors.

cards.mean: Ensures accuracy and completeness
cards.ex: Expected salary total NPR 200,000 compared with the processed total.

cards.mean: Ensures completeness
cards.ex: A meaningless total of employee IDs, used to see none are missing.

cards.mean: Ensures accuracy only
cards.ex: Age must be between 18 and 60.

cards.mean: Ensures accuracy only
cards.ex: An invoice cannot be above NPR 500,000.

cards.mean: Verification, validation, check digits, totals, range and limit checks
cards.ex: Check an invoice before it is accepted.

cards.mean: Program testing, test data and batch reconciliation
cards.ex: Compare batch totals before and after processing.

cards.mean: Error reports, exception reports, batch controls and distribution controls
cards.ex: Only authorised managers receive the salary report.

items.q: Comparing the entered amount with the original invoice
items.why: Comparing with a source document is verification.

items.q: The system rejects an age of 250
items.why: A programmed rule rejected it, so it is validation.

items.q: A check digit on a customer code
items.why: Check digits are a form of validation.

items.q: Matching entered data to the source documents
items.why: Source documents point to verification.

items.q: The system rejects an invoice above the set maximum
items.why: A programmed limit is validation.

topics.name: Validation lab
topics.line: Change the numbers and watch the checks accept or reject them.
topics.remember: Control total = accuracy and completeness. Hash total = completeness. Range and limit = accuracy only.
topics.simple: Try the checks yourself. Change the numbers and watch the system accept or reject them.
frames: The computer applies its programmed rule.
If it passes the rule, it is accepted.
If not, it is rejected, or the totals do not agree.
gls: the value must lie between a minimum and a maximum
the value must not pass a set limit
a meaningless total used to check completeness

items.q: Check digits
items.why: Check digits ensure accuracy.

items.q: Control totals
items.why: Control totals ensure both accuracy and completeness.

items.q: Hash totals
items.why: Hash totals ensure completeness.

items.q: Range checks
items.why: Range checks ensure accuracy only.

items.q: Limit checks
items.why: Limit checks ensure accuracy only.

topics.name: Backup and personnel controls
topics.line: Getting data back, and making fraud hard to hide.
topics.remember: Backup recovers lost data. Archive preserves history. Split duties so one person cannot control a whole transaction.
topics.simple: Even with every control, things can go wrong. Backups bring data back. People controls make fraud harder to hide.
frames: Archive keeps history. Backup recovers lost data.
A disaster recovery plan uses off-site storage.
Rotate jobs, enforce leave and split duties so one person cannot hide fraud.
gls: a copy used to recover data after a loss
stored history kept for future reference

cards.mean: At least daily
cards.ex: A nightly backup of the accounting database.

cards.mean: Preserve and retain historical information
cards.ex: Financial records of previous years.

cards.mean: Restore systems after serious disruption, with off-site storage
cards.ex: Backup copies at another location survive a fire.

cards.mean: Background and suitability checks
cards.ex: Checks before someone handles payroll data.

cards.mean: Move staff between duties periodically
cards.ex: Another person sees the work and may spot irregularities.

cards.mean: Require annual leave so someone else covers
cards.ex: The cover person may find hidden manipulation.

cards.mean: Record who logged in and what changed
cards.ex: A deleted supplier record is logged with user and time.

cards.mean: Managers review significant entries
cards.ex: A finance manager reviews large journals.

cards.mean: Split a transaction between people
cards.ex: One prepares, one approves, one releases the payment.

items.q: One person prepares, another approves, a third releases payments
items.why: Splitting a transaction between people is segregation of duties.

items.q: Staff are moved between duties from time to time
items.why: Periodically moving staff is job rotation.

items.q: An employee must take annual leave while someone covers
items.why: Requiring leave is an enforced vacation.

items.q: A record of who logged in and which record was deleted
items.why: A record of activity is a system log.

regions.label: Segregation of duties: no one person controls a whole transaction

topics.name: New technologies and risks
topics.line: Six technology risks and seven risks of introducing a new system.
topics.remember: O-I-P-A-E-S for technology risks. ELDSPEV for development risks.
topics.simple: New technology brings new risks. There are six technology risks and seven risks of introducing a new system.
frames: Obsolescence: costly technology may be outdated very soon.
Inexplicability: AI decisions may be too complex to explain.
Privacy: keep personal data only for legitimate purposes and time limits.
Systems development: a new system can disappoint, lose data or lower productivity.
gls: time to recover the cost of an investment

cards.mean: Technology becomes outdated very quickly
cards.ex: Reduce it: outsource, buy upgradeable technology, choose a shorter payback period.

cards.mean: AI algorithms too complex for humans to explain
cards.ex: A bank cannot explain why AI rejected a loan.

cards.mean: Legitimate purposes for holding data, and time limits for keeping it
cards.ex: Keeping customer data longer than allowed.

cards.mean: Staff skill gaps and threats to segregation of duties
cards.ex: One user can create, approve and release payments.

cards.mean: Confidentiality breaches and responsibility for AI
cards.ex: Pasting confidential statements into an external AI tool.

cards.mean: Risks when building and introducing a new system
cards.ex: Data lost when moving to a new ERP.

cards.mean: The system does not do what was expected
cards.ex: Expected to automate 90 percent of work but it automates 30 percent.

cards.mean: Employees are not ready
cards.ex: New payroll software with no training.

cards.mean: Data lost in migration
cards.ex: Supplier balances not transferred.

cards.mean: Inadequate technical support
cards.ex: The vendor ignores a critical ERP error.

cards.mean: Productivity falls during rollout
cards.ex: Bank reconciliation takes a day instead of two hours.

cards.mean: Dissatisfied staff leave
cards.ex: Experienced staff resign.

cards.mean: New systems may be more vulnerable
cards.ex: A new payroll application miscalculates overtime.

items.q: Technology bought for NPR 10 million is outdated within a year
items.why: Becoming outdated quickly is obsolescence risk.

items.q: An AI system makes a decision that nobody can explain
items.why: Humans cannot explain the decision: inexplicability.

items.q: A company stores customer information longer than necessary
items.why: Holding personal data too long is a privacy and data protection risk.

items.q: An automated payment system lets one employee do every payment step
items.why: Weakened segregation of duties is an automation risk.

items.q: An employee shares confidential financial data with an external AI tool
items.why: A confidentiality breach with AI is an ethical risk.

items.q: Historical accounting data is lost during ERP implementation
items.why: Data loss during implementation is a systems development risk.
